title: User Churn Prediction Model
text:
User Churn Prediction Model
Fintech  ·  Python · XGBoost · SHAP · SQL
Problem
At a high-growth fintech platform, we were losing roughly 18% of activated users within the first 90 days. Retention campaigns existed but were untargeted — every churned user got the same re-engagement email, regardless of why they left. The result: low response rates, high unsubscribe rates, and wasted campaign budget.
The goal was to build a model that could identify users at risk of churning before they churned, score them by risk level, and enable the CRM team to run differentiated interventions.
Defining Churn

title: User Churn Prediction Model
text:
users at risk of churning before they churned, score them by risk level, and enable the CRM team to run differentiated interventions.
Defining Churn The first challenge was definitional. For a payments platform, "churn" is non-contractual — users don't cancel; they just stop transacting. We defined churn as: no transaction in 60 days for users who had at least one transaction in their first 30 days of activation . This gave us a clean binary label and excluded new users still in the activation funnel.
Feature Engineering
We built a feature set around three themes, all computed on a rolling 30-day lookback window per user:
Recency & Frequency: Days since last transaction, transaction count, active days, session count.
Product Depth: Number of distinct features used (UPI, bill pay, investments, etc.), feature adoption velocity in first 14 days.

title: User Churn Prediction Model
text:

Product Depth: Number of distinct features used (UPI, bill pay, investments, etc.), feature adoption velocity in first 14 days. Payment Behaviour: Average transaction value, transaction success rate, payment method diversity, failed transaction ratio.
Engagement Signals: Push notification open rate, app session duration, customer support contacts.

from datetime import timedelta
def build_features(df_events, reference_date, lookback_days=30):
 cutoff = reference_date - timedelta(days=lookback_days)
 window = df_events[df_events['event_date'] >= cutoff].copy()

Model
We trained a gradient-boosted classifier (XGBoost) with 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Hyperparameters were tuned with Optuna. Class imbalance (~80:20 non-churn:churn) was handled via scale_pos_weight . We prioritised recall in the top two deciles — we'd rather flag too many at-risk users than miss them.

Precision @ top decile: 76%

Interpretability with SHAP
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was used to make the model actionable for the CRM team. Instead of a black-box score, each user got a risk score plus the top 3 drivers of their score. This told the CRM team why a user was at risk — enabling personalised messaging.

Deployment & Impact
The model was deployed as a weekly batch job. Every Monday, users were scored and the top two risk deciles were passed to the CRM platform with their SHAP-driven personalisation tags. Three CRM interventions were built:
Low feature usage: Triggered a "discover" flow highlighting unused features relevant to the user's transaction history.
High failed transaction rate: Triggered a support call from the payments team.
Recency drop: Triggered a cashback offer tied to a relevant use case.

title: User Churn Prediction Model

Recency drop: Triggered a cashback offer tied to a relevant use case. After 3 months of running the model-driven campaigns vs the old blanket approach: 22% reduction in 90-day churn in the targeted cohort, translating to approximately ₹8 crore in retained annual revenue.
Key Learnings
Churn definition matters more than model choice. Garbage labels → garbage predictions, regardless of algorithm sophistication.
Feature diversity beats feature count. 15 well-engineered behavioural features outperformed 200 raw event flags.
Interpretability is a business requirement, not a nice-to-have. The model only drove impact because CRM could act on the SHAP drivers.

title: Bayesian Marketing Mix Model
text:
Bayesian Marketing Mix Model
Growth & Marketing Analytics  ·  Python · PyMC · Bayesian Inference
Problem
The marketing team was spending across six channels — paid search, display, affiliates, email, push, and TV — with no reliable way to measure the true contribution of each. Last-click attribution (the default in their analytics stack) was heavily crediting paid search and undervaluing brand campaigns and TV, leading to systematic over-investment in lower-funnel spend and neglect of awareness channels.
The goal was to build a marketing mix model (MMM) that could attribute revenue to each channel accounting for carryover effects, saturation, and external factors like seasonality and competitor activity.
Why Bayesian MMM?

title: Bayesian Marketing Mix Model
text:
to each channel accounting for carryover effects, saturation, and external factors like seasonality and competitor activity.
Why Bayesian MMM? Traditional frequentist MMM (OLS regression) is fast but brittle with sparse data and correlated spend channels. A Bayesian approach lets us encode prior knowledge (e.g., "TV has a longer carryover than paid search") and get uncertainty estimates on every coefficient — which matter when recommending budget reallocation to a CFO.
Adstock Transformation
Marketing spend doesn't immediately convert — it has a carryover effect that decays over time. We model this with a geometric adstock transformation:
import numpy as np

title: Bayesian Marketing Mix Model
text:
immediately convert — it has a carryover effect that decays over time. We model this with a geometric adstock transformation:
import numpy as np def adstock(spend: np.ndarray, decay: float) -> np.ndarray:
 """Geometric adstock with decay rate between 0 and 1."""
 adstocked = np.zeros_like(spend, dtype=float)
 adstocked[0] = spend[0]
 for t in range(1, len(spend)):
 adstocked[t] = spend[t] + decay * adstocked[t - 1]
 return adstocked
# TV has a longer carryover; paid search decays quickly
tv_adstock = adstock(tv_spend, decay=0.6)
sem_adstock = adstock(sem_spend, decay=0.2)
Saturation (Diminishing Returns)
Doubling spend doesn't double response — each channel has a saturation curve. We model this with a Hill transformation, which captures the S-curve shape of diminishing returns:

title: Bayesian Marketing Mix Model
text:

 """Hill function: K = half-saturation point, n = steepness."""
 return x**n / (K**n + x**n)
# Each channel gets its own K and n, learned from data
tv_saturated = hill_transform(tv_adstock, K=500_000, n=2.5)
sem_saturated = hill_transform(sem_adstock, K=80_000, n=1.8)
Bayesian Model with PyMC
We used PyMC to estimate channel coefficients with regularising priors. The key advantage: each coefficient comes with a posterior distribution, giving us confidence intervals for attribution and budget recommendations.
import pymc as pm

 beta_sem = pm.HalfNormal("beta_sem", sigma=1)
 beta_email = pm.HalfNormal("beta_email", sigma=0.5)
# Seasonality component
 seasonality = pm.Normal("seasonality", mu=0, sigma=0.2, shape=52)
# Base revenue (intercept)
 intercept = pm.Normal("intercept", mu=log_revenue.mean(), sigma=1)
# Linear predictor

 + beta_tv * tv_saturated
 + beta_sem * sem_saturated
 + beta_email * email_saturated
 + seasonality[week_idx])
# Likelihood

With posterior distributions on each channel's ROI and its saturation curve, we ran a constrained optimisation to find the spend allocation that maximises expected revenue given a fixed total budget:
Reduce paid search spend by 18% (heavily saturated — operating past the inflection point).
Increase TV spend by 12% (below saturation, high carryover).
Increase affiliate spend by 22% (strongest marginal ROI at current spend levels).
Results
After reallocation based on model recommendations (validated with a phased geo-test):
31% improvement in blended marketing efficiency (revenue per ₹ of spend).
Reallocating ₹3 crore from over-invested paid search to TV and affiliates without reducing total revenue.

Key Learnings
Priors are a feature, not a crutch. Encoding domain knowledge (TV decays slowly) stabilises the model where data is sparse.
Uncertainty quantification is essential for budget decisions. A point estimate without a confidence interval is just a guess.
Always validate MMM recommendations with geo-tests before a full reallocation. Models can be wrong; markets will tell you.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
Growth Marketing  ·  Python · XGBoost · EconML · Causal Inference
I'd been running campaigns for years before I realised a basic mistake we were all making. We were optimising the wrong thing.
The propensity model would tell us who was likely to convert. Marketing would target those users. The campaign would launch, conversions would happen, ROI looked great in the deck. Then, on a slow afternoon, someone ran a proper holdout — sliced out 20% of the targeted segment, sent them nothing, watched what happened.
The holdout group converted at almost the same rate as the treated group. We hadn't moved anyone. We'd just bought conversions we already owned.
The right question isn't "who is likely to convert?" — it's "whose probability of converting goes up because of the campaign?" Propensity models can't tell you that. Uplift models can.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
to convert?" — it's "whose probability of converting goes up because of the campaign?" Propensity models can't tell you that. Uplift models can. The 2×2 nobody draws on a whiteboard
Once you reframe targeting around incrementality, the user base splits into four groups, not one. And only one of them is worth spending money on:
Persuadables ✓
Convert only if treated. This is your real ROI. Maybe 8–15% of any base.
Sure Things
Convert anyway. Targeting them is a tax on the P&L disguised as performance.
Lost Causes
Don't convert either way. At least they're cheap to be wrong about — until you scale them.
Do-Not-Disturbs ✗
Convert only if you leave them alone. Treating them destroys revenue. Everyone has these. Almost nobody finds them.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
you scale them.
Do-Not-Disturbs ✗
Convert only if you leave them alone. Treating them destroys revenue. Everyone has these. Almost nobody finds them. Propensity models collapse the first two groups into one ("likely to convert") and don't even know the fourth exists. That's the whole bug, and most teams ship the bug for years before noticing.
You can't shortcut the RCT
This is the part I want to be honest about. Uplift modeling isn't a clever algorithm trick — it's an experiment design problem with an algorithm at the end.
You need genuine treatment and control groups from a randomised assignment. Not "the people we targeted last quarter vs the people we didn't" — those groups are different by selection, and any model you train on them will confidently learn the selection bias and call it uplift.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
we didn't" — those groups are different by selection, and any model you train on them will confidently learn the selection bias and call it uplift. For a quarterly cross-sell campaign on ~500K eligible users, we structured a clean split: 350K treated, 150K held out completely. Stratified on tenure, product holdings, and last-90-day activity so the two arms weren't accidentally different. Conversions tracked over a 21-day window post-treatment.
It is genuinely painful to leave 30% of your eligible base untouched in a campaign. The CRM lead asked me twice if we really had to. We had to. Without the holdout, the model trains on observational data, and observational uplift is roughly as reliable as reading the future in tea leaves.
What I tried first (and abandoned)

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
trains on observational data, and observational uplift is roughly as reliable as reading the future in tea leaves.
What I tried first (and abandoned) My first attempt was the obvious one — a single XGBoost classifier with a "treated" feature flag, then look at the change in predicted probability when you flip the flag from 0 to 1. It's quick, you only train one model, and on paper it gives you a CATE per user.
It also doesn't work. The model learns the average treatment effect across the population and shrinks individual uplifts toward that average. The persuadables and sure things end up with nearly identical scores, which defeats the entire point. I spent two evenings convincing myself it was working before the Qini curve told me it wasn't.
The T-Learner — boring, but it works

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
the entire point. I spent two evenings convincing myself it was working before the Qini curve told me it wasn't.
The T-Learner — boring, but it works Settled on the T-Learner (Two-Model). Train one classifier on treated users only, train another on control users only, both predicting P(convert | features). Uplift per user = treated model's prediction − control model's prediction. It's almost embarrassingly simple. It also outperformed every more sophisticated thing I tried on this data.

df_control = df[df['treated'] == 0]
features = ['tenure_days', 'product_count', 'txns_30d', 'avg_txn_value',
 'last_login_days', 'tier', 'cohort_age', 'feature_depth']

 'last_login_days', 'tier', 'cohort_age', 'feature_depth'] model_t = XGBClassifier(max_depth=5, n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05,
 eval_metric='logloss').fit(df_treat[features], df_treat['converted'])
model_c = XGBClassifier(max_depth=5, n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05,
 eval_metric='logloss').fit(df_control[features], df_control['converted'])
def uplift_score(X):
 p_treat = model_t.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
 p_control = model_c.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
 return p_treat - p_control
df_all['uplift'] = uplift_score(df_all[features])
I also benchmarked the X-Learner from econml , which is supposed to handle imbalanced arms better. On our split (70/30) the AUUC gap was about 2%. Production code stays simple where it can; the T-Learner won by default.
Why AUC is the wrong tool here

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
our split (70/30) the AUUC gap was about 2%. Production code stays simple where it can; the T-Learner won by default.
Why AUC is the wrong tool here This is the trap most people walk into when they first build an uplift model: they want to validate it like a classifier. AUC, accuracy, precision-recall. None of those apply. You're not predicting a label; you're predicting a counterfactual. There is no ground truth label for "would this user have converted in the world where we didn't treat them?"
The right tool is the Qini curve . Order users by predicted uplift, descending. Plot the cumulative incremental conversions on the y-axis against the fraction of users targeted on the x-axis. Steep rise on the left = your top scores really are the persuadables. Flat line = your ranking is no better than random.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
targeted on the x-axis. Steep rise on the left = your top scores really are the persuadables. Flat line = your ranking is no better than random. Our model's Qini-AUUC was 0.038 . The standard propensity model — same features, same data, just predicting P(convert) — sat at 0.011 . The uplift ranking was roughly 3.5× better at identifying incrementally valuable users. That gap is the gap between "good model" and "model that actually changes how money gets spent."
The Do-Not-Disturb discovery
Here's the part I didn't expect. A measurable segment — about 6% of the eligible base — had negative predicted uplift. The model was telling us: don't touch these users; treatment makes them less likely to convert.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
of the eligible base — had negative predicted uplift. The model was telling us: don't touch these users; treatment makes them less likely to convert. My first reaction was disbelief. Marketing's first reaction was disbelief. We pulled the segment and looked at it. They were almost all high-tenure, high-engagement users with a heavy product history. The kind of users any propensity model would flag as top targets .
The hypothesis (later half-confirmed by a follow-up survey): these are loyal customers who don't think of the relationship as transactional. A cashback push reframes the relationship as transactional, and they back off — not by churning, but by skipping the action they were probably going to take anyway. Their baseline conversion rate is high. Our intervention dropped it by 4–7 percentage points.

Until we ran an uplift model, we had no idea this segment existed. We had been targeting them every quarter. The single highest-ROI thing the model did wasn't finding new converts — it was building a suppression list we didn't know we needed.
Operationalising it
Models that don't ship don't matter. We deployed this as a fortnightly batch job. Every other Monday, the eligible base got re-scored. The CRM platform received three tags per user:
Persuadable — send the campaign.
Sure Thing — skip; don't waste the spend.
Do-Not-Disturb — actively suppress from this campaign family.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting

Persuadable — send the campaign.
Sure Thing — skip; don't waste the spend.
Do-Not-Disturb — actively suppress from this campaign family. Lost Causes weren't surfaced at all — there was nothing for the CRM team to do with them. We didn't try to "win them back"; that's a different model with a different objective.
The CRM team adjusted their send logic and we ran the new strategy for a full quarter alongside a propensity-baseline cohort that didn't get the uplift treatment.
What changed
+19%
Incremental conversions vs propensity-targeted baseline

Wasted spend on Sure Things
~₹4 Cr
Annualised budget reallocated to higher-uplift segments
No incremental media budget. Same channels. Same creative. The only thing that changed was who got the message.
What I'd do differently
A few things, in hindsight:

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:

What I'd do differently
A few things, in hindsight: Run more holdouts, more often. One quarterly RCT is the minimum. Channel behaviour drifts, treatment effects drift, and a six-month-old uplift model targeting a population whose response curve has shifted is just a confidently wrong model.
Build the suppression list first. Do-Not-Disturbs are the biggest win and the easiest to action. The persuadable identification work is harder and has more downside if the model degrades. Start with the suppression list, prove it works, then layer in the targeting.

title: Uplift Modeling for Incremental Targeting
text:
work is harder and has more downside if the model degrades. Start with the suppression list, prove it works, then layer in the targeting. Don't oversell the segments to the team. "Persuadables" sounds clean on a slide. In reality it's the top 1–2 deciles of predicted uplift, with a lot of overlap between the segments at the boundaries. The model produces a ranked score, not a clean 2×2. Pretending otherwise erodes trust the first time a "Persuadable" doesn't convert.
The bigger reframing — and the thing I now believe is the most important shift any analytics team can make — is moving from predicting outcomes to predicting effects . Outcomes give you a model. Effects give you a budget reallocation.

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
Growth Marketing  ·  Python · Markov Chains · Shapley Values · BigQuery
Last-click attribution was making us look smart while we were leaking money. That's the honest summary.
Every conversion got 100% credit to whichever channel the user happened to click last. Paid search and direct were getting 58% of attributed conversions between them. Display was getting 4%. Email and social, single digits each. Marketing's budget review followed the credit, the budget was reallocated up the funnel, and a few quarters later we wondered why growth was decelerating despite holding spend steady.

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
the credit, the budget was reallocated up the funnel, and a few quarters later we wondered why growth was decelerating despite holding spend steady. The honest answer was buried in the data: the median converting user touched 4.3 channels over 11 days before converting. The first touch was almost never paid search. Display showed up early and often, then disappeared from the attributed credit because it rarely closed the click. We were rewarding the salesperson at the desk and starving the entire pipeline that walked the customer to the desk.
Last-click is a budget tax. The channels best at closing get rewarded, and the channels that make closing possible get starved. Run it long enough and you optimise yourself into a corner where the only thing you can buy is "the close."
Why the obvious heuristics don't fix it

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
Run it long enough and you optimise yourself into a corner where the only thing you can buy is "the close."
Why the obvious heuristics don't fix it Before going to a proper model, we ran the standard set of attribution heuristics and looked at the results side by side. None of them survived scrutiny:
Last-click — what we already had. Overcredits closers. Status quo we wanted to leave.
First-click — just flips the problem. Overcredits discovery, ignores nurture. We'd be over-budgeting display and under-budgeting search.
Linear — every touch gets equal weight. Defensible in a slide but arbitrary as a budget rule. Treats a brand impression and a high-intent retargeting click as identical.
Time-decay — exponential weight toward recent touches. Still arbitrary. Where does the decay rate come from? Nowhere. Someone picks 7 days because it feels right.

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
exponential weight toward recent touches. Still arbitrary. Where does the decay rate come from? Nowhere. Someone picks 7 days because it feels right. All four pick an attribution rule a priori and force the data to fit it. What we needed was the opposite — let the actual journeys decide which channels were doing work and which were freeloading.
Three months of journeys, stitched in BigQuery
The data was already there; nobody had pulled it together. Session-level events from BigQuery, three months of user-level paths, with channel attribution per session and a binary conversion flag. After sessionising and stitching, we had ~2.5 million unique user journeys capped at a 30-day lookback before the conversion event (or the end of the window for non-converters).

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
we had ~2.5 million unique user journeys capped at a 30-day lookback before the conversion event (or the end of the window for non-converters). WITH sessions AS (
 SELECT user_id, session_start, channel, converted
 FROM `growth.sessions`
 WHERE session_start BETWEEN DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) AND CURRENT_DATE()
),
journeys AS (
 SELECT
 user_id,
 STRING_AGG(channel, ' > ' ORDER BY session_start) AS path,
 MAX(converted) AS converted
 FROM sessions
 GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT path, converted, COUNT(*) AS users
FROM journeys
GROUP BY path, converted;
The shape of the data alone was eye-opening. About 14% of converters had journeys ≥7 touches. Around 8% touched the same channel three or more times before converting. Display appeared in 38% of converting journeys but got 4% of the last-click credit. The model wasn't going to surprise us by a small amount.

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
Display appeared in 38% of converting journeys but got 4% of the last-click credit. The model wasn't going to surprise us by a small amount. Markov chains — what it actually does
The intuition is simple, even if the math looks intimidating. Treat the user's journey as a walk between channel "states", ending at either Conversion or Null. Look at all observed journeys and count how often each transition happens — paid search → display, display → email, email → conversion. Normalise into a transition probability matrix.
Now ask the only question that matters: what happens to the overall conversion probability if I remove a channel entirely from the graph? That drop in conversion rate is that channel's removal effect — its true contribution to the system. Normalise across channels and you have attribution weights.

title: Multi-Touch Attribution Engine
text:
conversion rate is that channel's removal effect — its true contribution to the system. Normalise across channels and you have attribution weights. It's elegant because it respects the structure of the data without forcing a rule on it. A channel that only appears as the last click in 10% of journeys but as an essential middle step in 60% will get its actual due. Last-click would call it "weak"; the removal effect calls it "load-bearing."
import numpy as np
states = ['Start', 'PaidSearch', 'PaidSocial', 'Display', 'Email',
 'Organic', 'Direct', 'Referral', 'Conversion', 'Null']

numpy as np
states = ['Start', 'PaidSearch', 'PaidSocial', 'Display', 'Email',
 'Organic', 'Direct', 'Referral', 'Conversion', 'Null'] def transition_matrix(journeys):
 counts = np.zeros((len(states), len(states)))
 for path, converted in journeys:
 sequence = ['Start'] + path + (['Conversion'] if converted else ['Null'])
 for a, b in zip(sequence[:-1], sequence[1:]):
 counts[states.index(a), states.index(b)] += 1
 row_sums = counts.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
 return np.divide(counts, row_sums, where=row_sums > 0)
P_full = transition_matrix(journeys)
def conversion_prob(P):
 # Absorbing Markov chain — solve for P(reach Conversion | starting at Start)
 Q = np.delete(np.delete(P, [8, 9], axis=0), [8, 9], axis=1)
 R = P[:8, 8:]
 N = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(8) - Q)
 B = N @ R
 return B[0, 0]
base = conversion_prob(P_full)

removal_effects = {}
for ch in ['PaidSearch', 'PaidSocial', 'Display', 'Email', 'Organic', 'Direct', 'Referral']:
 P_minus = P_full.copy()
 idx = states.index(ch)
 P_minus[idx, :] = 0
 P_minus[idx, states.index('Null')] = 1 # route through Null
 removal_effects[ch] = (base - conversion_prob(P_minus)) / base
total = sum(removal_effects.values())
attribution = {ch: re / total for ch, re in removal_effects.items()}

Cross-check with Shapley Markov is elegant but it's still one method, and one method that disagrees dramatically with the status quo gets pushed back hard. So we ran a second, independent attribution approach using Shapley values — treat each channel as a "player," each journey as a "coalition," and the conversion as the payout. Shapley distributes credit based on each channel's marginal contribution averaged over all possible orderings.
Shapley is mathematically cleaner, but it's computationally expensive (factorial complexity), so we restricted it to the top 7 channels and used Monte Carlo permutation sampling for the rest.

The two methods agreed within ±3 percentage points on every single channel. Two independent pieces of mathematical machinery converging on the same answer — that was the moment I stopped worrying about whether the model was right and started worrying about whether marketing would believe it.

The trust test — a real holdout Here's the thing about attribution models: two methods agreeing with each other is necessary but it's not sufficient. They could both be confidently wrong in the same direction. The only way to ground-truth attribution is to actually change something and see if the world responds the way the model predicted.
The most contentious claim coming out of the model was that display was being undercredited by 2.5×. Marketing didn't believe it. The display team obviously loved it. I ran a geo-holdout lift test: pause display in 20% of geo regions for 4 weeks, hold every other channel's spend constant, and measure the gap in incremental conversion rate vs control geos.

That's the moment attribution stopped being a "model debate" and became a budget document.
What we did with it
Marketing operations rebuilt the channel ROI dashboard against Markov-weighted conversions instead of last-click. Budget reviews stopped being political — when the question is "what does the data say?" the answer doesn't depend on who owns which channel.

What I'd do differently
Three things: Attribution decays faster than you think. We re-fit the model monthly. That cadence held for about six months, then channel mix shifted and we had to move to fortnightly. Build the re-fit pipeline at v1, not v2. An old attribution model with confident outputs is more dangerous than no model at all.
Lift tests should be part of the cadence, not a one-off. One geo-holdout bought us credibility for two quarters. After that, marketing leadership wanted fresh proof. A small but continuous program of lift tests across channels is the lowest-cost way to keep an MTA model honest.

Replacing the dashboard cold made the change feel imposed; showing both made the change feel obvious.
The reframe that took me longest to internalise: attribution is not a measurement problem, it's a decision support problem. The model only matters if it changes a budget meeting. title: Revenue Simulation & Forecasting
text:
Revenue Simulation & Scenario Forecasting Engine
FP&A · Strategic Planning  ·  Python · Monte Carlo · NumPy · Plotly
Problem
Every quarter, the finance and strategy team needed to present revenue forecasts for 12, 24, and 36 months to the board. The existing approach was a spreadsheet with three fixed scenarios — bear, base, bull — where each scenario was a single point estimate derived by manually adjusting a few key assumptions.
The problem: single-point forecasts communicate false precision. A "₹500Cr ARR by Q4" projection carries no information about how confident you are, what assumptions drive that number, or what range of outcomes is plausible. Board decisions made on these numbers often carried unquantified risk.
Approach: Monte Carlo Simulation

title: Revenue Simulation & Forecasting
text:
or what range of outcomes is plausible. Board decisions made on these numbers often carried unquantified risk.
Approach: Monte Carlo Simulation Instead of three fixed scenarios, we built a simulation engine where each key driver is modelled as a probability distribution. Running 10,000 simulations samples from those distributions and produces a full distribution of revenue outcomes — including percentile ranges, tail risks, and sensitivity rankings.
Key drivers modelled:
New user acquisition (monthly): Normal distribution, mean and std derived from last 12 months.
Activation rate: Beta distribution (bounded 0–1), parameterised from historical funnel data.
Monthly churn rate: Beta distribution, with a seasonal component for Q1/Q3.
Revenue per active user (ARPU): Log-normal distribution (right-skewed, as a small % of users transact at high value).

title: Revenue Simulation & Forecasting
text:
a seasonal component for Q1/Q3.
Revenue per active user (ARPU): Log-normal distribution (right-skewed, as a small % of users transact at high value). Growth lever shocks: Occasional discrete events (new product launch, regulatory change) modelled as Bernoulli draws that multiply the base trajectory.
Simulation Engine
import numpy as np
def simulate_revenue(months: int = 24, n_sims: int = 10_000) -> np.ndarray:
 """Returns array of shape (n_sims, months) with monthly revenue."""
 rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
# Sample driver distributions once per simulation
 monthly_new_users = rng.normal(loc=25_000, scale=4_000, size=(n_sims, months))
 activation_rate = rng.beta( a=8, b=2, size=(n_sims, months))
 churn_rate = rng.beta( a=2, b=18, size=(n_sims, months))
 arpu = rng.lognormal(mean=4.5, sigma=0.4, size=(n_sims, months))

 arpu = rng.lognormal(mean=4.5, sigma=0.4, size=(n_sims, months)) revenue = np.zeros((n_sims, months))
 active_base = np.zeros(n_sims)
for t in range(months):
 new_activated = monthly_new_users[:, t] * activation_rate[:, t]
 active_base = active_base * (1 - churn_rate[:, t]) + new_activated
 revenue[:, t] = active_base * arpu[:, t]
return revenue
sims = simulate_revenue(months=36, n_sims=10_000)
# sims.sum(axis=1) gives total 36-month revenue per simulation
Outputs
From the 10,000 simulations we extracted:
Median (P50) forecast — the most likely outcome.
P10 / P90 confidence band — the range within which 80% of outcomes fall.
P5 tail risk — the "bad scenario" the board should plan for.
Tornado chart — sensitivity analysis showing which driver has the most impact on P50 revenue variance.

Sensitivity Analysis
The tornado chart from the sensitivity analysis surfaced a non-obvious insight: monthly churn rate had 2× the impact on 36-month revenue as new user acquisition rate . A 1pp improvement in churn was worth more than a 10% increase in acquisition volume.

This directly influenced Q3 planning: retention budget was increased by 30% while acquisition efficiency targets were tightened, rather than simply growing top-of-funnel spend.
Business Impact
Board presentations moved from three fixed scenarios to probability-weighted ranges — materially better risk communication.
Identified churn as the #1 revenue lever, leading to the churn prediction project and ₹8Cr in retained revenue.
FP&A team adopted the engine for all quarterly planning cycles. Re-planning time reduced from ~3 days to ~4 hours (just update distributions from actuals, re-run).
Key Learnings
Uncertainty is information. A P10–P90 range tells leadership more than a point estimate ever can.

text:
Payment Metrics Anomaly Detection
Fintech · Real-time ML · GCP
Python 
 Isolation Forest 
 statsmodels 
 BigQuery 
 Google Pub/Sub 
 Cloud Run
The Problem
At Razorpay's scale, payment success rate drops of even 1–2% represent tens of crores in failed transactions and direct merchant churn. The challenge: detecting these anomalies fast enough to act — before merchants notice, before support tickets spike, before the damage compounds.
The existing approach was manual: on-call engineers eyeballing dashboards. Mean time to detect (MTTD) was 25–40 minutes for most incidents. In payments, that's an eternity.
The Solution: Layered Anomaly Detection
The system runs two complementary detection methods in parallel, each suited to a different anomaly type:

title: Payment Metrics Anomaly Detection
text:
Solution: Layered Anomaly Detection
The system runs two complementary detection methods in parallel, each suited to a different anomaly type: Statistical Control Charts (CUSUM) — detects gradual drifts and sustained shifts. Excellent for catching slow-burn degradation (e.g., a bank's acceptance rate declining over 2 hours).
Isolation Forest — detects sudden multivariate anomalies by isolating outliers across payment success rate, volume, latency, and error code distributions simultaneously.
Architecture
Metrics flow from payment processing systems into Google Pub/Sub , are aggregated in 5-minute windows in BigQuery , and processed by a Cloud Run service that runs both detectors continuously.

def cusum_detect(series: list, threshold: float = 5.0, drift: float = 0.5) -> bool:
 """
 CUSUM control chart for detecting sustained shifts.
 Returns True if a significant change is detected.
 """
 mean = np.mean(series[:20]) # Baseline from first 20 observations
 std = np.std(series[:20])
cusum_pos, cusum_neg = 0, 0

cusum_pos, cusum_neg = 0, 0 for x in series[20:]:
 z = (x - mean) / (std + 1e-8)
 cusum_pos = max(0, cusum_pos + z - drift)
 cusum_neg = max(0, cusum_neg - z - drift)
if cusum_pos > threshold or cusum_neg > threshold:
 return True # Anomaly detected
return False

Alerts fire only when both detectors agree — this eliminates the false positive problem that plagues single-method systems. When both flag an anomaly, a Slack alert is sent with:

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
Published on: June 13, 2026  ·  8 min read
The first time I presented a CAC payback number to a leadership team, I said "six months" with total confidence. It was wrong in three different ways at once — and not one of them was an arithmetic error. The math was clean. The number was still a fiction. This is about the three traps hiding inside that one tidy figure, and what I report instead.
CAC payback is supposed to answer a simple question: after we spend money to acquire a customer, how long until that customer pays us back? Shorter is better — it means capital recycles faster and you can grow without constantly raising. It's one of the few unit-economics numbers a CFO and a growth lead will both nod at.

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
recycles faster and you can grow without constantly raising. It's one of the few unit-economics numbers a CFO and a growth lead will both nod at. The problem is that the textbook formula — CAC ÷ monthly revenue per customer — quietly smuggles in three assumptions that are almost never true.
~2× gap between blended and true paid CAC in a typical mixed-channel business
30–80% of "revenue" that isn't margin once you adjust for COGS
0 cohorts that actually behave like the blended average
Trap 1: Blended CAC hides what acquisition actually costs
Blended CAC is total sales and marketing spend divided by all new customers — including the ones who arrived organically, through word of mouth, SEO, or your existing brand. Those customers cost you (almost) nothing to acquire, and they drag the average down.

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
through word of mouth, SEO, or your existing brand. Those customers cost you (almost) nothing to acquire, and they drag the average down. That's fine if you only ever want to describe the past. It's dangerous the moment you use payback to decide how much more to spend . The next marginal customer doesn't come from your organic base — they come from paid channels, at the paid price. Planning growth on blended CAC is like budgeting your next road trip using your lifetime average cost per kilometre, most of which you walked.
Blended CAC ₹1,400
Paid-only CAC ₹2,800
Illustrative: a business where ~50% of new customers arrive organically. Same spend, very different decision-making number.
Trap 2: Pre-margin payback counts money you never keep

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
~50% of new customers arrive organically. Same spend, very different decision-making number.
Trap 2: Pre-margin payback counts money you never keep The textbook formula uses revenue . But a customer paying you ₹1,000 a month doesn't pay back ₹1,000 of acquisition cost a month — they pay back whatever's left after the cost of serving them. Payment processing, cloud, support, the discount you gave them, the rewards you funded. In fintech and commerce especially, gross margin can be a thin slice of top-line.
Payback has to be computed on gross margin per customer , not revenue. Skip this and you'll declare payback "achieved" while the customer is still deep underwater on a contribution basis.

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
per customer , not revenue. Skip this and you'll declare payback "achieved" while the customer is still deep underwater on a contribution basis. The corrected formula: Payback (months) = Paid CAC ÷ (Monthly revenue per customer × Gross margin %). Two adjustments — paid-only in the numerator, margin in the denominator — and the same business can move from a confident "6 months" to an honest "14."
Trap 3: The average cohort doesn't exist
Even with paid CAC and margin sorted, dividing by an average monthly margin assumes every customer pays at a steady, identical rate forever. They don't. Real cohorts have a retention curve: a chunk churns in the first few weeks, the survivors settle, and the curve flattens. Early churners may never come close to paying back what you spent to acquire them — and they're invisible in a single blended average.

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
flattens. Early churners may never come close to paying back what you spent to acquire them — and they're invisible in a single blended average. The honest version isn't a single number at all. It's a cumulative margin curve per cohort: spend on day zero, then track how much contribution margin that exact group has returned at month 1, 3, 6, 12. Payback is the month the curve crosses your CAC line. Sometimes it never does.
A worked example
Same business, same spend, three ways of looking at it. Watch the "payback" move:
Method CAC Monthly value Payback
Textbook (blended, revenue) ₹1,400 ₹1,000 rev 1.4 mo
Paid CAC, still revenue ₹2,800 ₹1,000 rev 2.8 mo
Paid CAC, gross margin ₹2,800 ₹350 margin 8.0 mo
+ cohort-weighted (early churn) ₹2,800 ~₹260 eff. ~11 mo

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
CAC, still revenue ₹2,800 ₹1,000 rev 2.8 mo
Paid CAC, gross margin ₹2,800 ₹350 margin 8.0 mo
+ cohort-weighted (early churn) ₹2,800 ~₹260 eff. ~11 mo Assumes 35% gross margin and meaningful first-90-day churn. The "real" payback is nearly 8× the headline number — driven entirely by which assumptions you make explicit.
The number didn't get worse. The number was always this. The reporting just got honest.
What I report instead
When I present acquisition economics now, the headline isn't a single payback month. It's three things:
Paid CAC, by channel. Blended goes in an appendix, clearly labelled, never in the decision.
A cumulative contribution-margin curve per cohort, with the CAC line drawn across it. You can see the crossing point — or its absence — instead of trusting a divide.

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
curve per cohort, with the CAC line drawn across it. You can see the crossing point — or its absence — instead of trusting a divide. The marginal payback on the last incremental spend, because that's what actually answers "should we spend more?"
None of this requires fancier tooling. It requires refusing to collapse a curve into a point until you've looked at the curve.
Where this is still wrong

title: The CAC Payback Trap: Why Your Payback Period Is Lying to You
text:
of this requires fancier tooling. It requires refusing to collapse a curve into a point until you've looked at the curve.
Where this is still wrong I'm honest about the limits. Cohort curves are backward-looking — a cohort acquired in a downturn or under a new pricing model may behave nothing like last year's. Attribution noise means "paid CAC by channel" is an estimate, not a measurement, especially once you account for the organic lift that paid spend itself creates. And payback says nothing about magnitude — a customer can pay back fast and still be worth very little. That last gap is exactly why payback needs a companion metric, which is its own can of worms.

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
Published on: June 11, 2026  ·  8 min read
Three-to-one is the number everyone quotes and almost no one computes correctly. "We're at 3:1 LTV to CAC" gets nodded through in board decks, pitch decks, and growth reviews as if it were a law of physics. It isn't. It's a ratio of two numbers that are each easy to inflate, and the inflation always runs in the flattering direction.
The appeal is obvious. LTV:CAC compresses an entire business model into one figure: for every rupee you spend acquiring a customer, how many rupees of lifetime value come back? Above 3, the lore says you're healthy and should spend more. Below 1, you're lighting money on fire. Clean, intuitive, board-friendly.
And mostly wrong, because three different errors hide inside that ratio — and unlike payback, where the traps are in the denominator, here they compound.

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
mostly wrong, because three different errors hide inside that ratio — and unlike payback, where the traps are in the denominator, here they compound. 3:1 the rule of thumb, repeated far more than it's verified
1.5–2× typical LTV overstatement from survivorship alone
∞ implied lifetime when you naively divide by churn — nobody lives forever
Where the 3:1 rule even came from
It's worth saying plainly: 3:1 is a heuristic from early-2010s US SaaS, where gross margins were 80%+, sales cycles were predictable, and capital was cheap. It was never a universal constant. Drop it onto a payments business at 30% margin, or a consumer app with brutal early churn, and the same ratio means something completely different. Borrowing the benchmark without borrowing the context is the first mistake. The next three are arithmetic.
Error 1: Survivorship bias in LTV

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
Borrowing the benchmark without borrowing the context is the first mistake. The next three are arithmetic.
Error 1: Survivorship bias in LTV The most common way to compute LTV is from your existing customer base — average revenue, average lifespan, of the people who are still here . But the customers still here are the ones who didn't churn. You're measuring the survivors and projecting their loyalty onto everyone, including the third who left in the first two months and contributed almost nothing.
Real LTV has to be computed on a full cohort from acquisition — survivors and casualties together — or it systematically overstates. The healthier your survivors look, the more the dead ones are dragging the true number down, unseen.
Error 2: A rupee in year three isn't a rupee today

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
healthier your survivors look, the more the dead ones are dragging the true number down, unseen.
Error 2: A rupee in year three isn't a rupee today LTV is, by definition, future money. Margin you'll collect in year two and three, if the customer stays and if the business is around to collect it. Future money is worth less than money in hand — that's not pessimism, it's the time value of money, and ignoring it is the same error as valuing a bond at the sum of its coupons.
You have to discount future contribution back to present value. The further out the cash flow and the riskier the business, the more aggressive the discount. Undiscounted LTV flatters long-lived-but-thin customers and makes a 5-year payback look the same as a 5-month one.

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
the more aggressive the discount. Undiscounted LTV flatters long-lived-but-thin customers and makes a 5-year payback look the same as a 5-month one. The worst offender: LTV ≈ ARPU ÷ churn. Plug in a 2% monthly churn and you get a 50-month "lifetime" of full-value revenue, undiscounted, on survivors only. Three compounding optimisms in a single short formula. It's the unit-economics equivalent of assuming a stock keeps its best-ever year forever.
Error 3: The blended ratio hides the losers
A company-wide LTV:CAC averages your best channel and your worst into one number. Referral customers might be 8:1; a particular paid channel might be 0.7:1 and actively destroying value. Blend them and you get a comfortable 3:1 that tells you nothing about where to spend the next rupee — and quietly green-lights the channel that's bleeding.

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
them and you get a comfortable 3:1 that tells you nothing about where to spend the next rupee — and quietly green-lights the channel that's bleeding. The ratio is only decision-useful per channel and per cohort . The aggregate is a vanity number.
A corrected worked example
Same customers, the naive ratio versus the honest one:
Step Naive Corrected
Lifetime value basis survivors only full cohort
Gross LTV ₹12,000 ₹7,400
Discounted to present value — ₹5,600
CAC basis blended ₹1,400 paid ₹2,800
LTV : CAC 8.6 : 1 2.0 : 1
Illustrative, but the direction is real: every correction pulls the ratio down, and the gap between "8.6:1, spend everything" and "2.0:1, be careful" is the difference between a good quarter and a bad year.
A ratio that can only move in the flattering direction when you cut corners isn't a health metric. It's a comfort metric.
What ratio to actually trust

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
ratio that can only move in the flattering direction when you cut corners isn't a health metric. It's a comfort metric.
What ratio to actually trust I don't throw LTV:CAC out — I make it earn its place:
Full-cohort LTV , casualties included, never survivors-only.
Contribution margin, discounted to present value — not undiscounted revenue.
Paid CAC, per channel — so the ratio guides the next rupee, not just describes the average.
A time horizon stated out loud. "3:1 over 24 months" is a claim you can check. "3:1" alone is a vibe.
Computed that way, a 2:1 can be genuinely excellent and a reported 6:1 can be a mirage. The number matters far less than the assumptions you were willing to write down next to it.
Where this is still imperfect

title: LTV:CAC Is Lying to You
text:
6:1 can be a mirage. The number matters far less than the assumptions you were willing to write down next to it.
Where this is still imperfect Discount rates are a judgement call, and reasonable people pick different ones. Full-cohort LTV needs cohorts old enough to have a real tail, which young companies simply don't have — so you're extrapolating, and extrapolation is where optimism creeps back in. And LTV:CAC, however carefully built, still ignores timing : a 3:1 that takes four years to realise is worse for a cash-constrained business than a 2:1 that pays back in six months. That's why I treat it as one panel of the dashboard, never the dashboard.

→ The CAC Payback Trap — the timing question this ratio ignores, taken apart.
→ Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision — putting these unit economics into a forward model.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
Published on: June 9, 2026  ·  9 min read
Most "data-driven" decisions are justified after the fact. We make the call, then build the deck that explains why it was obviously right. The real leverage — the thing I've spent a good chunk of my career doing — is the opposite: simulating the P&L impact of a decision before you commit, while you can still change your mind for free.
Pricing change, marketing-budget reallocation, a retention bet, a new market — these are all financial decisions wearing operational clothes. Each one moves the P&L through a chain of drivers, and the chain is usually knowable in advance. Not precisely. But well enough to tell a good bet from a bad one before you've spent the money.
3 scenarios minimum — base, bull, bear — never a single point estimate
1–2 inputs that usually drive most of the outcome variance

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
spent the money.
3 scenarios minimum — base, bull, bear — never a single point estimate
1–2 inputs that usually drive most of the outcome variance <1 day to build a driver model good enough to kill a bad idea
Start with drivers, not totals
The mistake I see most often is modelling the output — "revenue will grow 20%" — instead of the drivers that produce it. A driver-based model breaks the number into the levers you actually control or can forecast, so that when reality diverges you know which assumption broke.
Revenue isn't an input. It's customers × conversion × average order value × frequency. Margin isn't an input. It's revenue minus the costs that scale with it. Build the model as the chain, and a decision becomes a change to one or two links you can reason about.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
revenue minus the costs that scale with it. Build the model as the chain, and a decision becomes a change to one or two links you can reason about. # A driver-based P&L skeleton — deliberately simple
def monthly_pnl(new_users, conv, aov, freq, gross_margin,
 fixed_cost, variable_cost_per_order):
 orders = new_users * conv * freq
 revenue = orders * aov
 cogs = orders * variable_cost_per_order
 gross = revenue - cogs
 contrib = gross * gross_margin # after channel/processing
 op_profit = contrib - fixed_cost
 return {
 "orders": orders, "revenue": revenue,
 "contribution": contrib, "op_profit": op_profit,
 }
# A decision = a change to one or two inputs.
# A 10% price rise is aov *= 1.10 — and probably conv *= 0.96.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
contrib, "op_profit": op_profit,
 }
# A decision = a change to one or two inputs.
# A 10% price rise is aov *= 1.10 — and probably conv *= 0.96. That last comment is the whole game. A price rise doesn't just lift AOV — it usually dents conversion. The model forces you to write down the second-order effect instead of pretending it isn't there.
One number is a guess. Three is a decision.
Never present a single forecast. A point estimate hides its own uncertainty and invites false confidence. Run at least three scenarios — base, bull, bear — built by flexing the key assumptions to honest high and low values.
Scenario Conv. uplift Churn impact 12-mo op profit
Bear +2% +1.5pp −₹8L
Base +6% +0.5pp +₹14L
Bull +11% −0.2pp +₹41L
Illustrative scenario set for a hypothetical pricing decision. The spread — not the base case — is what tells you how much you're really risking.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
scenario set for a hypothetical pricing decision. The spread — not the base case — is what tells you how much you're really risking. The decision rule lives in the spread. If the bear case is survivable and the base case is good, you take the bet. If the bear case is fatal, the expected value barely matters — you can't afford to be wrong even once.
Sensitivity: find the one input that actually matters
Most models have a dozen inputs and one or two that move almost everything. Sensitivity analysis — flexing each input alone and measuring the swing in the outcome — tells you where to spend your remaining research time, and where precision is wasted effort.
Conversion uplift ±₹24L
Churn impact ±₹16L
AOV change ±₹7L
Fixed cost ±₹3L
Tornado-style sensitivity: how much 12-month op profit swings when each input is flexed across its plausible range, holding the rest at base.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
±₹3L
Tornado-style sensitivity: how much 12-month op profit swings when each input is flexed across its plausible range, holding the rest at base. The payoff: if conversion uplift swings the outcome by ₹24L and fixed cost by ₹3L, stop arguing about the cost line. Go pressure-test the conversion assumption — run a small experiment, pull a comparable, talk to someone who's done it. You've just turned "model everything" into "validate the one thing that decides it."
A model's job isn't to predict the future. It's to make your assumptions explicit enough to argue about before they cost you anything.
The honest part: where the model will be wrong
I tell every stakeholder the same thing: this model is wrong, the only question is whether it's wrong in a way that changes the decision. Three failure modes I watch for:

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
the same thing: this model is wrong, the only question is whether it's wrong in a way that changes the decision. Three failure modes I watch for: Behavioural feedback I didn't encode. A price rise that triggers a competitor response, or a budget cut that quietly tanks morale and output. Models capture mechanics, not reactions.
Correlated assumptions. In a real downturn, conversion drops and churn rises and AOV falls — together. Bear cases that flex one input at a time understate genuinely bad scenarios.
False precision. A model that outputs "₹14,28,400" invites a confidence the inputs don't support. I round hard and quote ranges, on purpose.

title: Simulating the P&L Before You Make the Decision
text:
precision. A model that outputs "₹14,28,400" invites a confidence the inputs don't support. I round hard and quote ranges, on purpose. None of that makes the exercise pointless. A model that's roughly right and explicit beats a gut call that's confidently wrong and unexaminable. The value was never the forecast — it was being forced to say out loud what you believe, and by how much, before the money moves.

text:
1929 → 2026 — The Next Great Reset
June 2026  ·  Geopolitics  ·  15 min read
Work in progress · being expanded
The structural set-up looks uncomfortably 1929. The exit won't. And the country that benefits most from how the exit plays out is probably India.
This is a piece I've been putting off writing because the conclusion sounds like a "buy India" pitch dressed up as macro analysis. The data made me write it anyway. I'll show the bullish case, the bearish case, and what I think is settled vs. what's open. None of this is investment advice. All of it is testable.
1. What 1929 actually was
The 1929 crash is misremembered as just a stock market event. It was a regime change.

1929 wasn't just a crash. It was the start of a 15-year reshuffle that ended with the dollar replacing the pound sterling as the world's reserve currency, the gold standard abandoned, the US becoming the world's industrial centre, and a multi-decade transfer of capital from the old empires to the new one. The shape of the global financial system in 1945 was unrecognisable from 1925.
Crashes don't just destroy value. They reorder where the value goes next.

What's similar is the set-up. What's different is the exit. The exit changes everything about where capital ends up.
No gold standard to come off. In 1929, currencies were anchored to gold. The crisis forced an unanchoring (1933 in the US, formally everywhere by 1971). In 2026, currencies are already unanchored — the next shock won't break a monetary regime; it will break a hegemonic one.
Multipolar finance is already here. Dollar share of FX reserves: 59% and declining. Euro: 20%. RMB: 2.5% but growing 4× in a decade. Gold reserves at central banks: highest absolute level since the 1970s. The world has already started diversifying without waiting for permission.

title: 1929 → 2026 — The Next Great Reset
text:
Gold reserves at central banks: highest absolute level since the 1970s. The world has already started diversifying without waiting for permission. Industrial capacity is in Asia already. In 1929, the US was the world's manufacturer. Today, the US is 16% of global manufacturing output. China is 31%. The "manufacturing centre" reshuffle that took 30+ years post-WW2 doesn't need to happen this time — it already happened.
Settlement rails are programmable. CBDCs, RMB-denominated settlement (now ~50% of China–Russia trade), UPI international linkages with 7+ countries — the infrastructure for non-dollar global trade exists in a way it simply did not in 1929 or 1971.
Demographics flipped. US, Europe, China, Japan all face shrinking working-age populations through 2050. India, Indonesia, Nigeria, Vietnam expand. The labour scarcity story re-routes capital alongside the geopolitical story.

The implication: the next crisis doesn't transfer hegemony to the next single power. It transfers hegemony to a basket — RMB for energy and East Asia trade, EUR for European integration, INR-pegged baskets for South Asia and Africa, gold and crypto as neutral reserves. The dollar doesn't collapse . It demotes.

The Bull Case for INR

Remittances cushion. $129B/year — largest in the world. This is structural, not cyclical.

The Bear Case for INR
Oil price shock. India imports 87% of its crude. A $20/barrel sustained spike adds ~$40B/year to the current account deficit.
RBI intervention bias. RBI has historically resisted INR appreciation to protect export competitiveness. Likely caps the rate of appreciation even if fundamentals support it.
Inflation differential. India CPI structurally ~3pp above US CPI. Purchasing-power parity arithmetic implies long-run depreciation against the dollar.

differential. India CPI structurally ~3pp above US CPI. Purchasing-power parity arithmetic implies long-run depreciation against the dollar. Capital flight risk. A global risk-off event would pull FII money out of India first. Saw this in 2008, 2013 taper tantrum, 2020.
Twin deficits. India still runs a current account deficit and fiscal deficit. A "twin-deficit" country structurally can't have a strong currency without external financing.
Geopolitical risk premium. India's neighbourhood (Pakistan, China, Bangladesh, Myanmar) attracts a risk premium that compresses currency valuation.
Both lists are factually correct. The argument isn't which is wrong; it's which dominates during a global financial reset . My take, with appropriate humility:
In a normal cycle, the bear case wins. INR drifts to 90–95 by 2030 on standard inflation-differential math. This is the consensus view.

Timing. The fragility is real. The trigger could be 6 months or 6 years away. Anybody claiming otherwise is selling something.

I'm cautious about prescriptive recommendations, but if you read this and want to act on the framing: Diversify USD exposure if you're heavily concentrated in it. The asymmetric downside on the dollar in any reset scenario is real.
Long-duration Indian assets — equities, sovereign debt, real estate in major cities — benefit disproportionately from any version of the bull case. The base case still does fine.

I've wanted to write this for a while. Every political debate about India's two decades collapses into anecdote, WhatsApp forwards, and selective statistics. Both sides cherry-pick. Neither is wrong about their chosen numbers. Both are hiding inconvenient ones.
So I decided to do the boring, unflattering version: compile 201 data points across twelve categories, note the source for each, and let the numbers speak.  76 944 ~1,300 (Jun 2026, incl 5G FWA) 
 +1,142% +38% 
 Mixed 
 Verdict revised to Mixed on saturation/ceiling grounds. Both eras grew subscribers, but the addressable market is structurally capped at ~1.0–1.1B (population minus children under ~10 and the very elderly). P1 grew into a virgin market (76M → 944M, capturing most of the addressable population in one decade). P2 inherited a near-saturated market (944M → 1,170M) where additional growth is mathematically constrained — almost the entire addressable population already had a SIM by 2014. The headline P1 advantage (+1,142% vs +24%) is real but is mechanically driven by the ceiling, not by policy quality. The substantive transition in P2 has been smartphones (~150M → 850M+), mobile data (UPI, OTT, e-commerce), and second-SIM penetration. Comparing raw subscriber growth across the two eras isn't apples-to-apples. TRAI ⟳ Aug 2026 update: TRAI: wireless (mobile + FWA) subscribers reached 1,300.25M at end-Jun 2026 (mobile-only 1,277M in May 2026). Published ~1,170 is stale. Saturation argument in existing note still holds; verdict Mixed unchanged. · TRAI telecom subscription report Jun 2026 (tele.net) · TRAI May 2026 data (Outlook Business) ⟳ Gap-closure analysis (Aug 2026): Against a ~1.4B population ceiling, P1 closed 66% of the remaining gap and P2 78% (ratio 1.19) — below the 1.5× threshold; Mixed stands under the saturation-adjusted rule too.

 Income ~0.37Wealth ~0.74 Income ~0.38Wealth ~0.77 Consumption ~0.255 (WB, 2022-23)Wealth ~0.83 (2024) 
 Slight rise income Sharp rise wealth 
 Mixed 
 Two very different pictures depending on which Gini you use. Income Gini (World Bank): India is among the world's 4th most equal countries by income distribution (~0.35), and has marginally improved under NDA — driven by DBT, rural welfare schemes, and MGNREGA continuity. Wealth Gini (~0.83) tells the opposite story: top 1% own 40% of wealth. However, the wealth inequality surge is a global phenomenon — driven by asset price inflation (stocks, real estate) post-2014 which lifted rich households everywhere. India's wealth Gini rise mirrors USA, UK, and China. Income equality is the fairer governance measure; wealth inequality is partly structural. WID / World Bank Gini ⟳ Aug 2026 update: Label fix, not a new number: the World Bank's headline 25.5 Gini (basis of the 'India among most equal' claim) is a CONSUMPTION Gini from HCES 2022-23, not an income Gini of ~0.35. World Bank API confirms SI.POV.GINI = 25.5 (2022), down from 28.8 (2011). Income Ginis (WID-based) are far higher (~0.47+) — the note should not conflate the two. Verdict Mixed unchanged.

title: Text-to-SQL with LLMs: What Actually Works
text:
Text-to-SQL with LLMs: What Actually Works
March 4, 2026  ·  Data & AI  ·  8 min read
The first version I built was embarrassingly bad. The LLM kept hallucinating column names, and once — I still think about this — it generated a DELETE statement because someone asked "remove the duplicates from my view." In production. Nearly ran it.
I've built a few of these systems since. Here's what I actually learned, not the sanitised tutorial version.
Why most demos are misleading
Every Text-to-SQL demo you see online uses a clean, three-table schema with sensible column names like customer_name and order_date . Real databases have columns named cust_id_v2_new , seven different tables that all have an id column, and a fact table someone built in 2019 that nobody fully understands anymore.
The gap between "works on the demo" and "works on your actual data" is where 90% of these projects die.

title: Text-to-SQL with LLMs: What Actually Works
text:
2019 that nobody fully understands anymore.
The gap between "works on the demo" and "works on your actual data" is where 90% of these projects die. The thing that matters most: your schema prompt
If I had to pick one variable that determines whether a Text-to-SQL system is good or useless, it's how you describe your schema to the model. Not the model you pick. Not the temperature setting. The schema description.
Most people dump CREATE TABLE statements into the prompt and call it done. That's not enough. You need to tell the model what the columns mean — business meaning, not just data types. And include sample values. The difference in SQL quality is not small.
def build_schema_prompt(db_connection):
 schema_parts = []
tables = db_connection.execute(
 "SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'public'"
 ).fetchall()

The system prompt that works for me I've tried a lot of variations. This is roughly the prompt structure I've settled on with Gemini — the key things are: be explicit about what you don't want, set the output format hard, and don't give the model wiggle room on destructive operations.
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a SQL expert. Generate a single valid {dialect} SQL query.
Database schema:
{schema}
Rules — follow these exactly:
- Return ONLY the SQL query. No explanation, no markdown, no backticks.
- Only use tables and columns that exist in the schema above.
- Never use DROP, DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT, ALTER, TRUNCATE under any circumstances.
- If the question is ambiguous, make the most reasonable assumption and proceed.
- Limit results to 500 rows unless the user is asking for aggregations.

If your database has 80+ tables, you can't fit everything in context and you shouldn't try. Build a retrieval step first — embed the question, find the 5-10 most relevant tables, and only send those to the model. This is just RAG applied to your schema.
Temperature. Use 0 or 0.1 for SQL. Higher values feel creative but produce queries with subtle logic errors that look plausible. I learned this the hard way — a temperature-0.7 query once returned the right number but calculated it wrong. Took me two days to catch.
What it costs

title: Text-to-SQL with LLMs: What Actually Works
text:
learned this the hard way — a temperature-0.7 query once returned the right number but calculated it wrong. Took me two days to catch.
What it costs With Gemini 1.5 Flash: a typical query with schema context is around 2,000 input tokens plus your question. At current pricing that's about $0.00015 per query — roughly $5/month at 1,000 queries a day. For most small-to-medium deployments this is noise.
When it's worth building and when it isn't
It works well when your schema is reasonably documented, your questions are fact-based ("how many users signed up last week?"), and you're aggregating over one or two tables. Internal analytics tools are the sweet spot.
It struggles with complex multi-table joins, questions that require knowing your specific business context ("what counts as an activated user in our system?"), and anything real-time where query cost matters.

If 70% of queries come back right without much iteration, you have something worth investing in. If you're constantly debugging hallucinated column names, the schema documentation problem needs solving first.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
text:
LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
March 4, 2026  ·  Data & AI  ·  7 min read
I want to be careful not to write the usual "AI is changing everything!" post. You've read those. They're mostly written by people who've spent more time thinking about AI than actually integrating it into analytical workflows.
I've spent the last year doing the second thing. At Razorpay and in side projects. Here's what I actually think.
Let's start with what doesn't work
LLMs don't fix bad data. This sounds obvious but I've seen teams reach for AI tooling as a way to avoid the harder work of data quality — and it doesn't work. The model confidently answers wrong questions with wrong data.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
text:
AI tooling as a way to avoid the harder work of data quality — and it doesn't work. The model confidently answers wrong questions with wrong data. They don't reason causally. Ask an LLM "did this campaign cause the revenue lift?" and it will give you a confident, well-structured answer. That answer is a guess dressed up as analysis. For causal questions you still need experimental design, proper controls, and causal inference. The LLM can help you write the code for that — it cannot replace the thinking.
They also don't know your business. They don't know that your December data is always noisy because of year-end cleaning, or that user_id 0 is a test account, or that "activated" means something different in your product than the industry definition. That institutional context lives in people's heads and in your code, and no amount of prompting gets around its absence.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
text:
the industry definition. That institutional context lives in people's heads and in your code, and no amount of prompting gets around its absence. Where they actually help — five things I use regularly
1. EDA, faster. Exploratory data analysis is the most important and most tedious part of the job. Loading data, checking distributions, looking for nulls and outliers, finding obvious correlations. With a good coding assistant, I do this in a third of the time I used to. The value isn't just speed — it's that I end up exploring more. When iteration is cheap, you ask more questions.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
text: in a third of the time I used to. The value isn't just speed — it's that I end up exploring more. When iteration is cheap, you ask more questions. 2. SQL for non-technical stakeholders. The highest-leverage near-term use case, and the one I'd recommend most teams start with. Product managers and growth leads have data questions they never ask because the friction of "file a ticket with analytics" is too high. A decent Text-to-SQL tool collapses that friction. The analytics team's job shifts from writing queries to building the system and handling the hard questions. That's the right direction.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building

Weekly business reviews. Monthly reports. Anomaly alerts. Someone has to translate numbers into sentences — and it's usually the analyst, which is a waste of their time for routine reporting. I've built a system at work that takes the week's key metrics, passes them to Gemini with enough context, and generates a 3-4 sentence Slack summary automatically. Took a day to build. Saves a few hours a week.

4. Classifying free-text data at scale. This one unlocks something genuinely new. Support tickets, NPS comments, cancellation reasons — we've always collected this data and almost never analysed it systematically because it's time-consuming to classify manually. Analytics codebases are badly documented. LLMs are good at explaining what a complex SQL transformation does and adding useful comments. Not glamorous, but it matters — especially for anything that other people need to maintain.
The shift in what the job looks like
Here's what I notice changing in my own work: I spend less time on the mechanical translation parts — question to query, data to chart, numbers to sentences — and more time on the harder stuff. Defining what question is even worth asking. Catching the places where data is misleading. Designing experiments properly.

title: LLMs for Analytics: Honest Take After a Year of Building
text:
time on the harder stuff. Defining what question is even worth asking. Catching the places where data is misleading. Designing experiments properly. I think this is the real change. Not that AI makes analysts redundant — it makes the boring parts of the job smaller, which means more time for the parts that actually require judgment.
Whether that's a good thing depends on whether you find the boring parts of analytics frustrating or comfortable. Honestly, some people prefer the predictability of writing a known query to the ambiguity of doing genuine analytical thinking. That's fine — but it's worth being honest about which camp you're in, because the job is shifting.
Where to start if you haven't yet
